results.corrected_extracted: Clinical review for clinicians by four clinical pharmacists (schools of pharmacy in Kansas, Arkansas and California). PubMed and Google Scholar were searched for English-language literature from 1946 to 2016 with the keywords urine drug test, screen, false-positive, false-negative and abuse and individual drug names, with references cited in retrieved papers added; only publications on urine testing in humans or human samples were kept; the numbers of records and the selection steps are not reported, and no method for appraising the cited studies is described (the text comments on the evidence for some agents only).
results.note: Search details confirmed on pp. 1-2. 'Not appraised' was too absolute: the text qualifies some evidence (one case report for proton pump inhibitors, lamotrigine without confirmation, no evidence for amoxicillin), though no formal appraisal is described.

results.corrected_extracted: Table 2, 'Approximate Drug Detection Time in the Urine', adapted from the authors' 2008 review, gives one value per row with no cutoff, test or amount (only marijuana and synthetic cannabinoids are split by pattern of use): alcohol 7–12 hours; amphetamine 48 hours; methamphetamine 48 hours; barbiturates, short-acting (pentobarbital) 24 hours, long-acting (phenobarbital) 3 weeks; benzodiazepines, short-acting (lorazepam) 3 days, long-acting (diazepam) 30 days; cocaine metabolites 2–4 days; marijuana, single use 3 days, moderate use (4 times a week) 5–7 days, chronic use (daily) 10–15 days, chronic heavy smoker more than 30 days; codeine 48 hours; heroin (morphine) 48 hours; hydromorphone 2–4 days; methadone 3 days; morphine 48–72 hours; oxycodone 2–4 days; phencyclidine 8 days; synthetic cannabinoids, single use 72 hours, chronic use more than 72 hours; synthetic cathinones variable. Its nine sources (references 9–17) are a 1987 report of a Council on Scientific Affairs in JAMA, a 2004 review of urine testing in pain medicine, a textbook on psychoactive drugs, the authors' 2008 review, two laboratory web pages answering questions on synthetic cannabinoid testing, a psychiatry textbook chapter, Verstraete (2004) and a 2005 article in a pharmacists' newsletter. The text calls these standard detection times and says detection depends on half-life, metabolites, interactions, dosing interval, amount, chronic or occasional use, time of last use, body mass, urine pH and concentration, and kidney or liver impairment.
results.note: Every value checked on the 300-dpi rendering and references 9-17 on p. 18. Only change: 'one value per drug with no ... conditions' is not exact, since marijuana and synthetic cannabinoids carry values by pattern of use.
Cutoff paragraph (pp. 2-3) and every Table 1 value checked on the 300-dpi rendering.

results.corrected_extracted: Screening immunoassays for cannabis react to several THC metabolites (federal cutoff 50 ng/mL; some laboratories may use a lower cutoff of 20 ng/mL); confirmation by GC-MS or LC-MS/MS is specific for THCCOOH, with a federal cutoff of 15 ng/mL. Detection depends on route, amount and potency, frequency of use, body mass and metabolic rate; chronic use leads to THC accumulating in fat and slow elimination, so cannabis can be detected in urine for more than 30 days after stopping in people who used chronically, whereas a single exposure in people who do not use it is typically detectable for up to 72 hours.
results.note: Hedge restored: the source says some laboratories 'may use' 20 ng/mL. Everything else matches the 4th and 5th paragraphs on p. 5.

results.corrected_extracted: Clinical review for clinicians by four clinical pharmacists. PubMed and Google Scholar were searched for English-language literature from 1946 to 2016 with the keywords urine drug test, screen, false-positive, false-negative and abuse and individual drug names, plus references cited in retrieved papers; only publications on urine testing in humans or human samples were kept; the numbers of records and the selection steps are not reported, and no method for appraising the cited studies is described (the text comments on the evidence for some agents only). The introduction says that misreading a result (false positive or false negative) can have significant consequences, such as loss of a job or incarceration.
results.note: Same change as n 1 ('not appraised' too absolute). The introduction sentence on consequences is confirmed on p. 1.
Highlights and the 2nd to 4th paragraphs of Methods of Drug Testing on p. 2 match, including the contrast between the highlights and the clinical-judgment wording in the text.
Table 4 checked on 300-dpi renderings of pp. 6-7, footnotes included. My recount also gives 33 amphetamine-screen entries. Reference 12 is Moeller, Lee and Kissack (2008), Mayo Clin Proc.

results.corrected_extracted: Amphetamine immunoassays are the screens most commonly associated with false positives, which the authors attribute to other cross-reacting drugs and substances, adding that antibodies specific to amphetamine and methamphetamine are hard to develop because of their structures; the assays detect amphetamine, dextroamphetamine, methamphetamine, MDA, MDEA and MDMA. Agents commonly linked to false-positive amphetamine results are pseudoephedrine and ephedrine, bupropion, labetalol and ranitidine; metformin has also been linked; selegiline is metabolized to l-methamphetamine and l-amphetamine; lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) is converted to d-amphetamine and will be detected; in a Department of Defense analysis, the supplement ingredient DMAA was found in 92.3% of the false-positive amphetamine samples that GC-MS then confirmed negative.
results.note: Attribution fixed: the source gives cross-reacting drugs and substances as the reason, and states the antibody difficulty as a separate sentence. All other items, including 92.3%, match pp. 12-13.

Text matches pp. 11-12. Editors' note checked: Moeller reference 53 is Blank et al. (2009) and 59 is Röder et al. (2007). Saitman PDF p. 4 reports both other point-of-care tests negative, Drug Screen Multi 5 included. Saitman never cites Röder.

results.corrected_extracted: Medicines reported to cross-react with cannabis immunoassays include proton pump inhibitors (evidence limited to one pantoprazole case report and its package insert), NSAIDs (in Rollins et al., 2 of 510 samples gave false positives for cannabis, one from a patient taking ibuprofen daily and one from a patient taking naproxen long term; interference appears rare) and efavirenz (well documented; attributed to its glucuronide metabolite). Several baby wash products, investigated because false-positive THC screens in newborns had increased, gave dose-dependent responses on THC immunoassays, many positive at a 20 ng/mL cutoff and none reaching the standard 50 ng/mL.
results.note: The review never says the baby wash responses were measured in newborns' urine. Newborns are only the reason Cotten et al. tested the products. Everything else matches the 8th to 11th Cannabinoids paragraphs on p. 8.

results.corrected_extracted: True positives from medicines: dronabinol, a synthetic THC, tests positive for THC and cannot be told apart from plant THC by confirmatory tests, whereas nabilone tests negative (p. 7); codeine is metabolized to morphine and norcodeine, all three detectable in urine after codeine, and codeine and hydrocodone metabolism can produce small amounts of hydrocodone and hydromorphone respectively, which should not be read as use of those drugs when high concentrations of codeine or (as printed) hydromorphone are detected (p. 10); lisdexamfetamine is converted to d-amphetamine and is detected (p. 13).

results.corrected_extracted: Coca leaves used in teas, drinks and other products in some countries can make cocaine screens positive. Cocaine screens test for benzoylecgonine and show minimal cross-reactivity; the claim, repeated by internet sources and review articles, that amoxicillin causes false positives lacks evidence, and Reisfield et al. found no false-positive results for cocaine metabolites with amoxicillin on 4 immunoassays; cocaine used as a topical anaesthetic in ear, nose and throat or eye procedures can give true positives, while benzocaine, lidocaine, procaine and tetracaine, being structurally distinct, do not produce false positives.
results.note: Hedge restored: topical and ophthalmic cocaine 'can produce' true positives. The rest matches the 1st and 2nd Cocaine paragraphs on p. 13.

PCP 2nd to 5th paragraphs on p. 14 match: the 24%, 22% and 15% with no stated denominator, the single ketamine case against 3 self-reported negatives, venlafaxine, and lamotrigine in 2 patients without confirmation.

results.corrected_extracted: Incidental exposure to alcohol through hand sanitizers or mouthwash can produce positive urine test results; in the same paragraph the metabolite ethyl glucuronide is the preferred test because it can be detected in urine for 2 to 5 days after drinking, and a ratio of ethyl glucuronide to ethyl sulfate may help tell drinking from incidental exposure.
results.note: The source says incidental exposure can give 'positive UDT results' and does not name ethyl glucuronide tests as the ones affected. That link is only implied by the paragraph.

key_findings.correction: Approximate urine detection times (Table 2): alcohol 7-12 hours; amphetamine and methamphetamine 48 hours; barbiturates, short-acting (pentobarbital) 24 hours, long-acting (phenobarbital) 3 weeks; benzodiazepines, short-acting (lorazepam) 3 days, long-acting (diazepam) 30 days; cocaine metabolites 2-4 days; marijuana, single use 3 days, moderate use (4 times a week) 5-7 days, chronic use (daily) 10-15 days, chronic heavy smoker more than 30 days; codeine 48 hours; heroin (as morphine) 48 hours; hydromorphone 2-4 days; methadone 3 days; morphine 48-72 hours; oxycodone 2-4 days; phencyclidine 8 days; synthetic cannabinoids, single use 72 hours, chronic use more than 72 hours; synthetic cathinones variable. Note: adapted from the authors' 2008 review; its nine sources (references 9-17) are mostly secondary; no cutoff, assay or amount is given for any value, and only marijuana and synthetic cannabinoids are split by pattern of use. [The table says 'chronic heavy smoker', not 'daily'; the note's 'no ... condition' overlooked the use-pattern rows.]

Cannabis testing: screening immunoassays detect several THC metabolites (federal cutoff 50 ng/mL; some laboratories may use a lower cutoff of 20 ng/mL), and GC-MS or LC-MS/MS confirmation is specific for THCCOOH at a federal cutoff of 15 ng/mL; detection depends on route, amount and potency, frequency of use, body mass and metabolic rate; with chronic use THC accumulates in fat and its metabolites are eliminated slowly, so urine detection can last more than 30 days after stopping in people who used chronically, whereas a single exposure in people who do not use cannabis is typically detectable for up to 72 hours. [Hedge restored: 'may use'.]

Cannabis, recent versus past use: glucuronides of THC and 11-OH-THC were studied as markers of use within the last 8 hours, but Lowe et al. found them (concentrations of these markers, by context) in urine up to 24 days after a person who used heavily stopped, which the review says refutes their usefulness; THC was detectable in blood after 30 days in 5 people (Bergamaschi et al.), and blood THC can fall quickly within the first hour. [The source does not say 'THC' was found in urine at 24 days.]

Prescribed cannabinoids: dronabinol (synthetic THC) tests positive for THC and cannot be told apart from plant THC by confirmation, while nabilone tests negative; a urine test for the plant cannabinoid THCV, meant to separate cannabis from dronabinol, was positive in only 50% of participants who used cannabis heavily (5 times per week, as printed) (Levin et al.). ['At least' is not in the source.]

Cannabis screens and medicines or products: proton pump inhibitors (evidence limited to one pantoprazole case report and its package insert), NSAIDs (Rollins et al.: 2 false positives in 510 samples, one with daily ibuprofen and one with chronic naproxen use; called rare) and efavirenz (well documented; its glucuronide metabolite) are reported to cross-react; several baby wash products, investigated because false-positive THC screens in newborns had increased, gave dose-dependent responses on THC immunoassays, many positive at a 20 ng/mL cutoff and none reaching 50 ng/mL. [The review does not say the responses were in newborns' urine.]

Opiate and methadone screens and medicines: ofloxacin was positive on the EMIT II opiate assay at a 300 ng/mL threshold while norfloxacin and ciprofloxacin were not (Meatherall & Dai); gatifloxacin gave a positive at 2000 ng/mL in a case report; rifampin has also caused false positives; verapamil, diphenhydramine and doxylamine have been reported to cause false-positive methadone screens; codeine can produce small amounts of hydrocodone, and hydrocodone of hydromorphone, which should not be read as use of those drugs when high concentrations of codeine or (as printed) hydromorphone are detected; hydromorphone is also a minor metabolite of morphine. Locator: Opioids, 5th, 7th and 10th paragraphs; Table 4 (pp. 6-7). [The 'reported' hedge and the condition were missing, and the paragraph numbers were one too high.]

Table 4, other screens: alcohol, short-chain alcohols such as isopropyl alcohol; benzodiazepines, efavirenz, oxaprozin, sertraline (may not detect alprazolam, clonazepam, lorazepam); cannabinoids, baby wash products, dronabinol, efavirenz, NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors (may not detect nabilone, synthetic cannabinoids); cocaine, coca leaf tea and topical anaesthetics containing cocaine; opioids, dextromethorphan, diphenhydramine and doxylamine (methadone assays only), heroin, opiates, poppy seeds, quinine, quinolones, rifampin, verapamil (methadone assays only); phencyclidine, dextromethorphan, diphenhydramine, doxylamine, ibuprofen, imipramine, ketamine, lamotrigine, MDPV, meperidine, mesoridazine, thioridazine, tramadol, venlafaxine and O-desmethylvenlafaxine; tricyclic antidepressants, cyclobenzaprine and quetiapine, and carbamazepine, cyproheptadine, diphenhydramine and hydroxyzine (serum only, footnote f); synthetic cannabinoids, lamotrigine. [Footnote f is also on carbamazepine.]

Cocaine screens test for benzoylecgonine and have minimal cross-reactivity; the claim that amoxicillin causes false positives lacks evidence (Reisfield et al. found no false positives on 4 immunoassays); coca leaf teas, drinks and other products can make cocaine screens positive, and topical or ophthalmic cocaine can give true positives; benzocaine, lidocaine, procaine and tetracaine do not cause false positives. [Both statements are hedged with 'can' in the source.]

Synthetic cathinones: attempts to detect them in urine have not given good results; validation studies of one commercial immunoassay (Randox Drugs of Abuse V biochip) found mephedrone and MDPV concentrations below acceptance criteria with a high negative bias; parent cathinones are excreted rapidly in urine, with an elimination half-life of about 12 hours, and urine pH can influence the amount excreted. Synthetic cannabinoids are not detected by cannabis tests; little parent drug reaches urine; most assays target JWH-018 and JWH-073 metabolites; there is no accepted cutoff (assays 5-25 ng/mL); in Barnes et al., several of 73 synthetic cannabinoids cross-reacted, raising the cutoff from 5 to 10 µg/L increased false negatives by 12%, newer compounds (PB-22, RCS-4, RCS-8, XRL-11, AKB48) were poorly detected and none of 93 common medications and metabolites cross-reacted; laboratories estimate detection for 48 to 72 [hours] after last use. [The source does not say 'the only' assay validated; pH is said to affect the amount excreted, not the half-life.]

reporting_issues.correction: Units are µg/L on the 300-dpi rendering of p. 13; reference 175 is Smith et al. (2014), J Anal Toxicol.
Checked against Saitman et al. PDF p. 4 and Moeller references 53 and 59.
The review describes 6 non-smokers under three conditions (p. 8). The 18 participants, 6 per session, come from the project's card sc_cone_2015; the primary paper is not on file.

issue: Table 2 gives single values without cutoff, assay or amount (only marijuana and synthetic cannabinoids are split by pattern of use), from mostly secondary sources (references 9-17); it also gives 48 hours for heroin (as morphine) but 48-72 hours for morphine, while the text gives 6-acetylmorphine only up to 8 hours. | consequence: The values are approximate and second-hand; they should not be presented as the detection time of a particular test.

risk_of_bias.note: I agree with the design (narrative review), the instrument (none applicable) and overall high risk: selection is unsystematic and the tables are second-hand. The domain notes match the text (for example, 226 references, and reference 153 co-authored by Atayee).

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is fair. The text hedges weak evidence, while the tables and highlights are firmer than the evidence behind them.

missed: Urine detection times are said to be longer than in blood or serum, '1 day up to several weeks' (PDF p. 2, Methods of Drug Testing, 1st paragraph).
The most common reasons for false-negative opioid results are a test that is wrong for the specific opioid, or too little drug in the urine (PDF p. 10, Opioids, 4th paragraph).
Many methadone immunoassays detect only the parent drug and not the EDDP metabolite; one assay (HEIA) detects both (PDF p. 10, Opioids, 10th paragraph).
Locators: the card counts Opioids paragraphs as if the unindented right column of p. 9 began a new one. The same off-by-one appears in the anchors (key findings 11-13).
